mcqs.q: Tooth eruption is defined as:
opts: Axial/occlusal movement of a tooth from its developmental site to its functional position
mcqs.explain: Eruption is the axial (occlusal) movement of a tooth (or germ) from its developmental position in the jaw to its functional position in the oral cavity.

mcqs.q: Passive eruption refers to:
opts: Apical recession of the gingiva exposing more tooth (no tooth movement)
Active movement of the tooth into the arch
mcqs.explain: Passive eruption involves no tooth movement; it is the apical recession of gingival tissue that exposes more tooth structure. Active eruption is the actual movement of the tooth.

mcqs.q: The three phases of eruption are:
mcqs.explain: The phases are pre-eruptive, eruptive (prefunctional) and post-eruptive (functional).

mcqs.q: The pre-eruptive phase begins at the ___ and ends at ___:
opts: Early bell stage; crown completion (start of root formation)
mcqs.explain: The pre-eruptive phase begins in early crown formation (early bell stage) and ends at crown completion (the start of root formation); all movement occurs within the crypts.

mcqs.q: During bodily (pre-eruptive) movement of a tooth germ:
opts: Bone is resorbed ahead of the germ and deposited on the crypt wall behind it
Bone is deposited ahead and resorbed behind
mcqs.explain: In bodily movement, bone is resorbed on the surface toward which the tooth moves and deposited on the crypt wall behind it.

mcqs.q: Eccentric growth of a tooth germ means:
opts: One part remains stationary while the rest grows, shifting the germ's centre
The germ rotates around its long axis
mcqs.explain: Eccentric growth is where one part of the germ remains stationary and the remainder continues to grow, leading to a shift in its centre.

mcqs.q: Permanent molars (no deciduous predecessor) begin development in the:
opts: Maxillary tuberosity / mandibular ramus, then tilt upright
Lingual plate of the anterior bone
mcqs.explain: Maxillary permanent molars develop in the tuberosity (occlusal surfaces facing distally) and mandibular molars in the ramus (facing mesially), then tilt upright with jaw growth.

mcqs.q: The eruptive (prefunctional) phase runs from:
opts: The beginning of root formation to reaching occlusion
Crown completion to root completion only
mcqs.explain: The eruptive (prefunctional) phase starts at the beginning of root formation and ends when the tooth reaches occlusion; the rate of eruption exceeds jaw growth.

mcqs.q: The small bony canal connecting a permanent tooth's crypt to the surface, guiding eruption, is the:
mcqs.explain: The gubernacular canal connects the successor's crypt to the surface (lingual plate anteriorly, deciduous-molar socket for premolars), guiding eruption.

mcqs.q: The gubernacular cord contains:
opts: Remnants of the dental lamina and connective tissue
mcqs.explain: The gubernacular cord (within the gubernacular canal) contains remnants of the dental lamina and connective tissue; both canal and cord provide the directional path of eruption.

mcqs.q: In the tissues overlying the erupting tooth, the roof of the crypt is removed by:
mcqs.explain: Osteoclasts resorb the bone in the roof of the crypt, while the connective tissue between the reduced enamel epithelium and oral epithelium degenerates.

mcqs.q: As the tooth approaches the surface, the reduced enamel epithelium:
opts: Fuses with the oral epithelium, and central cells degenerate to form a canal
mcqs.explain: The reduced enamel epithelium fuses with the oral epithelium forming a central mass; the central cells degenerate (aided by desmolytic enzymes), creating an epithelial-lined canal through which the tooth erupts.

mcqs.q: Tooth eruption is normally painless because of:
opts: Degeneration of the overlying connective tissue, fewer vessels and broken nerve fibres
Absence of any nerves in the jaw
mcqs.explain: Eruption is painless due to degeneration of the overlying connective tissue, a decrease in blood vessels and the breakdown of nerve fibres.

mcqs.q: Blanching of the mucosa over an erupting tooth is caused by:
opts: Stretching and thinning of the mucosa (REE fused to oral epithelium)
mcqs.explain: Fusion of the reduced enamel epithelium with the oral epithelium stretches and thins the overlying mucosa, causing blanching; the epithelial-lined canal allows eruption without bleeding.

mcqs.q: The post-eruptive (functional) phase:
opts: Begins when the tooth reaches the occlusal plane and lasts the life of the tooth
Is the same as the bud stage
mcqs.explain: The post-eruptive (functional) phase begins when the tooth reaches the occlusal plane and continues for the life span of the tooth.

mcqs.q: To compensate for proximal (interproximal) wear, the tooth undergoes:
mcqs.explain: Mesial drift compensates for proximal wear; axial movement compensates for occlusal wear and maintains position as the jaws grow.

mcqs.q: To maintain its position as the jaws increase in height, a tooth uses:
mcqs.explain: Axial movement maintains the tooth's position as the jaws grow in height and compensates for occlusal wear.

mcqs.q: Which is a proposed theory/cause of tooth eruption?
mcqs.explain: Proposed theories include root formation, bone remodelling, dental follicle proliferation, PDL traction and pulpal/vascular pressure.

mcqs.q: The most important causes of eruption are considered to be:
opts: Root elongation, alveolar bone modification, and PDL modification
mcqs.explain: The most important causes are elongation of the root, modification of the alveolar bone and modification of the periodontal ligament, coupled with overlying tissue changes.

mcqs.q: Pre-eruptive tooth movements occur:
opts: Within the bony crypts, before root formation begins
mcqs.explain: All pre-eruptive movements occur within the crypts of the developing crowns, before root formation begins.

mcqs.q: During the eruptive phase, the rate of tooth eruption is:
opts: Greater than the rate of jaw growth
mcqs.explain: In the eruptive phase the rate of tooth eruption is greater than the rate of jaw growth, allowing the tooth to reach the occlusal plane.

mcqs.q: Movement of a tooth around its longitudinal axis is termed:
mcqs.explain: Rotatory movement is around a longitudinal axis; tilting is around a transverse axis; axial is along the long axis; bodily is translation in one direction.

saqs.a: Active: actual movement of the tooth from its developmental site to the arch. Passive: apical recession of gingiva exposing more tooth (no tooth movement).

saqs.q: When does the pre-eruptive phase begin and end, and where does movement occur?
saqs.a: From the early bell stage to crown completion (start of root formation); all movement is within the crypts (bodily + eccentric growth).

saqs.q: List the four events of the eruptive (prefunctional) phase.
saqs.a: Root formation, occlusal movement through the crypt, penetration of the crown tip through the epithelium, and intra-oral movement to occlusion.

saqs.q: What are the gubernacular canal and cord?
saqs.a: The gubernacular canal connects the successor's crypt to the surface; the gubernacular cord (dental-lamina remnants + CT) within it guides the eruption path.

saqs.q: Describe the changes in the tissues overlying the erupting tooth.
saqs.a: Osteoclasts resorb the crypt roof; CT degenerates; the reduced enamel epithelium fuses with the oral epithelium; central cells degenerate forming an epithelial-lined canal (bloodless eruption).

saqs.q: Why is tooth eruption painless and bloodless?
saqs.a: Painless: CT degeneration, fewer vessels, broken nerves. Bloodless: the tooth erupts through a pre-formed epithelial-lined canal.
Axial movement to maintain position (jaw growth) and compensate occlusal wear; mesial drift to compensate proximal wear.
